[h1]It's really hard to talk about TLD. Is it a good driving sim? Not really. Is it a good survival game? Nope. Is it a game I enjoy? Yes. [/h1]

Personally, I would call The Long Drive the "Subway Surfers of exploration games". Every individual gameplay element and mechanic in this game is held together with hot glue and boogers yet together they form a cacophony of an addictive gameplay loop that makes you wonder why you even like playing it to begin with.
[hr][/hr]
I can't say I particularly enjoy the driving in this game. At best it's solid every time the physics don't bug out and outright kill you, at worst the cars handle like a fridge barreling down a hill. The first major issue comes from the vehicles being practically weightless - the occasional pothole you hit will send the vehicle tumbling and potentially destroying hours of progress through no fault of your own, or the car can just explode from hitting seemingly nothing at all (which, in most cases, is remedied by enabling the interior physics lock). The other major issue comes from a very rudimentary terrain generation the game is using. There's just you, the road and an occasional barrier or a structure; nil variety gets boring after a while making the driving feel unengaging and limiting the potential for exploration.
While the survival elements lay a fairly solid groundwork their presence is hindered by the lack of risk or balance. You're not very likely to die of starvation or dehydration as the game's loot generation system is basic and non-dynamic; combined with the fact that there's nothing stopping you from stockpiling food and water in the trunk of your car, it creates very little incentive to interact with the world once you hit a certain point.
[hr][/hr]
So, why exactly am I recommending this game? The weird mix of car mechanic and nomadic journey gameplay elements creates an open-ended gameplay loop that tickles my fancy that I can't yet pin down why. The Long Drive doesn't have that much of a plot and most things are there as throwaway gags which creates a very eerie and unique vibe. It's the type of game to be enjoyed with your friends, while drinking or listening to a podcast. 

Even though the updates are rolled out at a snail's pace the devs are still trying to keep the game fresh by adding new content and bugfixes, so I'm hoping to see this project grow and fix the aforementioned issues.

[h1]Enormous potential, very charming[/h1]

That's the quickest, best way to describe [i]The Long Drive.[/i] Let's be clear, at the time of writing, the game is Early Access and is broken in lots of hilarious and annoying ways. However, the idea it presents is what makes me want to keep playing and see where it goes. 

The game combines a lot of the themes I enjoy. If you're anything like me and you enjoy old Top Gear Specials, The Grand Tour, documentaries on dangerous roads and anything post-apocalyptic, you'll find something to enjoy here. The Long Drive gives you all of those. It's pretty clear the team behind the game is small and they're definitely having some fun with it. That said, I hope the game doesn't fall too deep into [i]novelty[/i] to lose sight of what it [i]could be[/i].

The car maintenance, the scavenging, the looming threat all make you feel like you're the star in your own road film. When I first got my blue station wagon cleaned up and in working order I was so proud of it. Begrudgingly I moved onto a bus - a bigger project. Over time I managed to fix her up too but I struggled with fuel. Just like those Top Gear Specials I mentioned, I didn't know what I was running on - it was fumes. I find a garage that has a broken down car. I start piecing it together again using what is to hand, odd parts and missing doors and I am reminded of Jeremy Clarkson driving across Africa in his broken and beaten up Lancia. One problem though, no gas. So I hop back into my bus and hope for the best.

Then I saw it,[spoiler]a ship in the desert[/spoiler]. I frantically search the remains and pull together piles of useful materials. Wedging barrels into stairwells of the bus to stop them rolling around really shows how the physics of the game make it so much more engaging than an inventory system. 

Later, I find a storehouse loaded with junk. I sift through and filter bits of fluids and other materials into useful piles on the sand outside my bus as the sun sets. I walk round changing wheels and cleaning parts. Somewhere between Mad Max, Fallout and Test Drive I've just realised I'm still playing at [b]4:00am.[/b]

Among the debris I found a radio and after many hours of silent travelling I finally have some company. I am amazed that the first radio station is playing the sort of music I like; it's a synthwave station. Now I am driving along at dusk, gazing out the side of the bus windows, watching giant rabbits run along the desert, all scored with dreamy synthwave. [b]This is brilliant[/b]. Again, I'm reminded of the montage shots in Top Gear or The Grand Tour. 

It is worth mentioning too that all the radio stations are excellent. The music is all [i]genuinely good[/i] and the narrator, although similar across the board, I assume given their resource availability, is also amusing - there is a real GTA tongue-in-cheek vibe to everything that is said. 

I really connected with this game and I really hope it gets the support it deserves. I think there is ultimately three things the game needs now:

[b]It needs polish:[/b] collision detection, building functionality, texture popping, multiplayer. 

[b]It needs variety:[/b] many more vehicles, locations, buildings, parts, collectables, environmental features.

[b]It needs more modes:[/b] you can drive a long way but I would love to see a survival mode. Food and water requirements, scavenging for things in the desert, making additions to your chosen building/home, boarding up windows, defend against [spoiler]aliens[/spoiler] and more. We know multiplayer is being worked on. Imagine frantically fuelling a bus as your friends fight off bunnies? Fantastic.

Best of luck Genesz.

This game is like if you put a road in a bunch of out-of bounds scenery and were told to survive. It is bizarrely relaxing to embark on this infinite road trip with a friend.

[h1]So far, I've spent 8 hours with this game, I can't say I didn't enjoy them. However, due to the state this game is currently in I decided not to recommend it, and here is why.[/h1]

So first off, the concept is rather geniuine. Sure, road tripping games have been made before, such as Jalopy- which I consider the best one out there, and it's lame knock off- Road To Guangdong. There's also this Under The Sand thing, but from what I heard it's currently abandoned.. 
None of these games offer what this one does- endless driving through the world you're put into with next to minimal car maintenance, by which I mean all you have to take care of is your oil, fuel and coolant level, I think tire condition also matters, but they don't seem to degrade, so once you find 4 good tires you don't have to worry about them anymore. Cars also handle pretty good, I like how suspension actually reacts to road it's on. You can also do interesting things to your vehicle, run it on alcohol (though it won't get you too far..), get rid of it's parts freely or customize it in a limited way. (I heard that more options to customize your cars are planned)

[h1]That said, I'll explain why this game isn't worth buying, yet.[/h1]

The reason is simple, technical and content issues. The Long Drive currently lacks content to the point where you have basically seen everything after 2 hours of gameplay. I managed to count 4 POI's that you can visit and explore, and a few useless ones that are there only to enhance the landscape. Buildings containing loot are usually very empty, and have nothing to offer aside from items scattered around them..
You get to drive 3 cars, thing is, they don't really differ much from each other. Sure, the Trabant based car requires you to mix oil with fuel so it can run, this isn't correct from the technical side as it should start anyway, albeit with a risk of damaging the engine but I guess there has to be a workaround if there [b]is no engine damage[/b]. Yep, you can't damage vehicles in this game in any way, previously mentioned oil and coolant levels will only stall the car if they get too low. 
Then, there's this game's sense of humor.. It mainly consists of radio host joking about sex, burping, peeing and sh!tting.. You can also find a sex doll in this game. I don't think anyone older than 7 will find this funny, I'd somehow understand ability to take a dump anywhere if it served some purpose, but currently it doesn't..
[i]haha mom look fart poo funny ;DDD[/i]
Right now once you find enough gas (which is like 10L) and top up your coolant and oil, you can drive forever as cars burn very little fuel and lose rest of the fluids very, very slowly. This is where the game pretty much ends.. Something like a survival mode(by which I mean needs like hunger, thirst, ect.) or basic vehicle repairs would be great for this game, it'd actually give you a reason to continue your journey.

And now onto technical issues this game suffers from..

One major complaint I got with this game is it's physics. If you think My Summer Car physic engine is funky, then you should see what this one does. Putting items into the glovebox is basically saying goodbye to them, your car's trunk isn't much diffrent, but a bit safer.. 
Cars like to suddenly freeze while driving and then launch themselves forward, which usually leads to a crash.. Did I mention that rolling over or even spinning out makes all of your items fly out of your vehicle? and it doesn't happen rarely, it literally happens every 5 minutes. 
There are also cactus plants growing on roads, and rocks placed randomly on them. 
I could run this game at stable 60fps, so framerate is not an issue here.
Controls in this game are very weird, you can get used to them, but they're far from being good, or even intuitive.. and no, they can't be changed, hence I'm saying this.

[h1]Final words..[/h1]
Overall, The Long Drive is a game that's worth following, but not buying, just yet. The devs are keen on interacting with community and releasing updates, so it's very likely that a lot of issues I mentioned here will be adressed in near future. I'll write a new review for this game once it changes to something better.

The Long Drive is a game that I recommend, kind of. It has a very interesting concept that I and many other people love, and with the game being as beautifully scuffed as it is, playing with friends or alone can be absolutely hilarious. However, the game CURRENTLY sits in a state of limbo. It has not received a single update in 3 years (although beta tests have been released, with the newest being just about a year old at the time of writing this review) and there has been barely any communication from the dev. Ever since its release in 2019 the game has been plagued with the issue of spaghetti code. Spaghetti code is code that is written in a very inefficient manner, and it has had a huge effect on the game as a whole. The code is so inefficient that it brings very capable computers to their knees. The multiplayer is very fun to play but can suffer from very severe desync issues, and in its current state is not worth playing. There also are some AI generated paintings being used within the game, they are difficult to notice at they match the vibe of the game very well, but they are still there.

In the game's CURRENT state, I cannot recommend it to anyone.

However, in contrast to what many reviewers are saying the game is NOT abandonware! The reason why there has been no updates in the past 3 years is because the spaghettified state of the game's code makes it next to impossible to update and maintain. As a result, Genesz (who is the game's only developer) has started rewriting the entire game's code from scratch, which includes a new game engine and improvements to the game's performance. This process is taking much longer than initially anticipated to complete, and this has led to many people viewing the game as abandonware. If this new update rolls out and the game is playable and operates well, then I definitely recommend it to anyone who is interested in the game!

After watching an undisclosed individual play this game, I decided to dish out some cash and check it out for myself. I feel there are some great features in The Long Drive despite the technical limitations derived from the physical and graphical aspects of the game; however, I will try to avoid commentary on these issues wherever possible, as they seem self-evident. Instead, I will focus on the elements that the developer sets out to achieve in this project and two parts that I happened to favour most of all in this context.

First, the world: in what I have seen from this game so far, the simulated environments in The Long Drive provide a decent attempt at the sensation of hitting the road despite the aforementioned issues; however, I will give particular encouragement and praise to the random elements that, I feel, could be improved to present this as the centrepiece for the future development of this game. Adding a greater pool and variety of random events (i.e. derelict structures, small towns, gas stations, diners, government experimental sites, etc.) with some subtle and humorous scenes with a short story would make for some interesting and engaging experiences, perhaps leading onto some more interesting development projects, such as procedural generation and emergent narrative, for use in this game and future games.

Second, the driving and the vehicles: another critical element in this game is how this feature interacts with the current environment, again, despite the aforementioned issues. I particularly liked the customisation options (i.e. exchanging vehicle parts, bodywork, accessories, maintenance), giving players more freedom, choice and engagement in the world, which are objectives cited by the developer. I can only encourage this to diversify further.

Overall, and in conclusion, The Long Drive is an ambitious project with a lot of promise to set out to achieve its goal, yet there is more work to be done; my fear is that if the physical and graphical issues of the game are pandered to, then the development will stall on the features with the most promise. On this basis, I would encourage the developer to spend time on diversifying the environment and interactive elements that provide more freedom, choice and engagement.

I've wanted a game like this since childhood: driving endlessly in a car through a desert, stopping at occasional points of interest to loot them. If you enjoyed flying infinitely out of bounds in the GTA series or other games that allowed it, you'll love this game. It delivers that feeling perfectly. I also enjoyed the car physics and its interactions. it's definitely a game made by people who love these aspects. However, there's not much other content to offer. You'll experience most of it in the first 10 hours, and after that, it's just driving as far as you can. The game is quite junky too, but not in a broken, rather fun way, so i don't mind it. Multiplayer could breathe new life into this game, but it's almost unplayable right now. Developers are reportedly working on rewriting core parts of the game to improve its performance. So, for now, only buy it if you're looking for long, autistic driving by yourself.
